summary.text: Taking \(n=2\) and \(p=2\), direct evaluation of the defining products gives \(a(4)=1\), so \(\operatorname{ord}_2(a(4))=0\). However, the proposed sum is \(\sum_{i\ge0}\left\lfloor\lfloor2/2^i\rfloor/2\right\rfloor=1\), since only the \(i=0\) term is nonzero.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(N)=\frac{\displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^{N}\prod_{k=1}^{N}\gcd(j,k)}
{\displaystyle\prod_{k=1}^{N}\bigl(\lfloor N/k\rfloor!\bigr)^k}.
\]
For a prime \(p\), write \(\operatorname{ord}_p(m)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in the prime factorization of the positive integer \(m\). The conjecture asserts that, for every positive integer \(n\) and every prime \(p\),
\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np))
=
\sum_{i\ge 0}\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor n/p^i\rfloor}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
We disprove this by taking
\[
n=2,\qquad p=2.
\]
These values satisfy all the hypotheses: \(n\) is positive and \(p=2\) is prime. Since \(np=4\), we first compute \(a(4)\) directly from its defining products.

For the numerator, group the factors according to the first index \(j\). For \(j=1,2,3,4\), respectively, the row products are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\prod_{k=1}^{4}\gcd(1,k)
 &=1\cdot1\cdot1\cdot1=1,\\
\prod_{k=1}^{4}\gcd(2,k)
 &=1\cdot2\cdot1\cdot2=4,\\
\prod_{k=1}^{4}\gcd(3,k)
 &=1\cdot1\cdot3\cdot1=3,\\
\prod_{k=1}^{4}\gcd(4,k)
 &=1\cdot2\cdot1\cdot4=8.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
\prod_{j=1}^{4}\prod_{k=1}^{4}\gcd(j,k)
=1\cdot4\cdot3\cdot8=96.
\]

The denominator is
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{4}\bigl(\lfloor4/k\rfloor!\bigr)^k.
\]
Its four factors are
\[
\begin{aligned}
k=1 &: \quad (\lfloor4/1\rfloor!)^1=(4!)^1=24,\\
k=2 &: \quad (\lfloor4/2\rfloor!)^2=(2!)^2=4,\\
k=3 &: \quad (\lfloor4/3\rfloor!)^3=(1!)^3=1,\\
k=4 &: \quad (\lfloor4/4\rfloor!)^4=(1!)^4=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus this product is also
\[
24\cdot4\cdot1\cdot1=96.
\]
It follows that
\[
a(4)=\frac{96}{96}=1.
\]
Since no positive power of \(2\) divides \(1\), the actual value on the left-hand side of the conjectured identity is
\[
\operatorname{ord}_2(a(2\cdot2))=\operatorname{ord}_2(a(4))
=\operatorname{ord}_2(1)=0.
\]

Now evaluate the proposed right-hand side. It is
\[
\sum_{i\ge0}\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor2/2^i\rfloor}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
For \(i=0\), since \(2^0=1\), the summand is
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor2/1\rfloor}{2}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac{2}{2}\right\rfloor=1.
\]
For every \(i\ge1\), one has \(2^i\ge2\), so
\[
0\le \left\lfloor\frac{2}{2^i}\right\rfloor\le1.
\]
Dividing either possible value, \(0\) or \(1\), by \(2\) and taking the floor gives zero. Hence every summand with \(i\ge1\) vanishes. Therefore
\[
\sum_{i\ge0}\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor2/2^i\rfloor}{2}\right\rfloor=1.
\]

For \(n=2\) and \(p=2\), the conjecture would therefore require the false equality
\[
0=\operatorname{ord}_2(a(4))
=
\sum_{i\ge0}\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor2/2^i\rfloor}{2}\right\rfloor
=1.
\]
Thus \((n,p)=(2,2)\) is a counterexample, and the conjecture is false.
